kids.text: Introduction
Branch of electricity dealing with charges at rest
Electromagnetic forces underlie everyday forces: friction, tension, normal force
Historical background: Thales (amber), Benjamin Franklin (positive/negative)
Basic Properties of Electric Charge
Electric charge: intrinsic property of matter; SI unit: Coulomb (C)
Two types: Positive (+) and Negative (–); like repel, unlike attract
Conservation of charge: total charge in universe is constant; charge cannot be created or destroyed
Quantisation of charge: q = ne; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (Millikan's experiment)
Triboelectric charging: charging by rubbing (e.g., glass rod with silk)
Detection: Gold-leaf electroscope
Coulomb's Law
F = kq₁q₂/r²; k = 9 × 10⁹ Nm²C⁻²
Vector form: F₂₁ = –F₁₂ (Newton's 3rd law)
Permittivity of free space: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²N⁻¹m⁻²
Superposition Principle: net force = vector sum of individual forces
Electric Field
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge); unit: NC⁻¹ or Vm⁻¹
Electric field due to point charge: E = kq/r²
Electric Field Lines
Start from positive charge; end at negative charge
Never cross each other
Density of lines ∝ strength of field
Cannot form closed loops in electrostatics
Superposition: E_net = ΣEᵢ (vector sum)
Electric Dipole
System of two equal and opposite charges separated by distance 2a
Dipole moment: p = q × 2a; direction: –q to +q; unit: Cm
Electric field on axial line: E_axial = (1/4πε₀)(2pr)/(r²–a²)²; direction along p
Electric field on equatorial plane: E_eq = (1/4πε₀)(p)/(r²+a²)^(3/2); direction opposite to p
For r >> a: E_axial = 2E_eq; both vary as 1/r³
Torque on dipole: τ = pE sinθ; in vector form τ = p × E
Potential energy: U = –pE cosθ = –p·E
Electrostatic Potential
V = W/q (work done per unit charge); scalar quantity; unit: Volt (V)
Potential due to point charge: V = kq/r
Relation between E and V: E = –dV/dr (negative gradient of potential)
Equipotential Surfaces
No work done moving charge along surface
Always perpendicular to field lines
For point charge: concentric spherical surfaces
Electrostatic potential energy: U = kq₁q₂/r (for two charges)
Electric Flux and Gauss's Law
Electric flux: Φ = E·A = EA cosθ; unit: Nm²C⁻¹
Gauss's Law: Total flux through closed surface = Q_enclosed/ε₀
Applications of Gauss's Law
Infinite line charge: E = λ/(2πε₀r)
Infinite plane sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀)
Uniformly charged sphere: E = kQ/r² (outside), E = 0 (inside)
Electrostatic Properties of Conductors
Electric field inside conductor = 0 in electrostatic equilibrium
Charge resides only on outer surface of conductor
E at surface = σ/ε₀ (perpendicular to surface)
Potential is constant throughout conductor
Corona discharge: ionization of air near sharp points due to high E
Dielectrics and Polarisation
Dielectrics: non-conductors; polar (e.g., water) and non-polar (e.g., O₂)
Polarisation: induced dipole moment per unit volume; P = χₑ·ε₀·E
Dielectric constant (εᵣ): ratio of field without to with dielectric
Capacitance and Capacitors
Capacitance: C = Q/V; ability to store charge; unit: Farad (F)
Parallel plate capacitor: C = ε₀A/d (without dielectric)
With dielectric: C = εᵣε₀A/d = κC₀
Combination of Capacitors
Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ... (same charge, different voltages)
Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ + ... (same voltage, different charges)
Energy stored: U = ½CV² = Q²/2C = ½QV
Energy density: u = ½ε₀E²
Van de Graaff Generator
Generates very high voltages (millions of volts)
Working: corona discharge transfers charge to large hollow sphere
Applications: particle accelerators, nuclear physics research
Electric Current
I = dQ/dt; rate of flow of charge; unit: Ampere (A)
Conventional current: direction of positive charge flow (opposite to electrons)
Drift velocity: vd = eEτ/m; average velocity of electrons under E field
I = nAevd; n is free electron density
Ohm's Law and Resistance
V = IR; voltage is proportional to current for ohmic conductors
Resistance: R = ρl/A; ρ is resistivity; unit: Ohm (Ω)
Resistivity: ρ = m/(ne²τ); depends on material and temperature
V-I characteristics: linear (ohmic) vs non-linear (non-ohmic, e.g., diode)
Effect of temperature: R = R₀(1 + αΔT); α is temperature coefficient
Carbon Resistors and Colour Code
Four-band colour code: first two bands = digits, third = multiplier, fourth = tolerance
Colour sequence: BBROYGBVGW (0–9)
Combination of Resistors
Series: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃; same current, voltages add
Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃; same voltage, currents add
EMF and Internal Resistance
EMF (ε): work done per unit charge by source; unit: Volt
Terminal voltage: V = ε – Ir (during discharge)
Cells in series: ε_eq = nε, r_eq = nr
Cells in parallel: ε_eq = ε, r_eq = r/n
Kirchhoff's Rules
Current Rule (Junction Rule)
ΣI = 0 at any junction (conservation of charge)
Current entering = Current leaving
Voltage Rule (Loop Rule)
ΣV = 0 around any closed loop (conservation of energy)
Sum of EMFs = sum of IR drops in a loop
Wheatstone's Bridge and Applications
Balanced condition: P/Q = R/S; galvanometer shows zero deflection
Metre Bridge: based on Wheatstone's principle; measures unknown resistance
Potentiometer: measures EMF and internal resistance; no current drawn from source
Comparison of EMFs using potentiometer: ε₁/ε₂ = l₁/l₂
Electric Power and Energy
Power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R; unit: Watt (W)
Electrical energy: E = Pt = VIt; unit: Joule (J) or kWh
Heating Effect – Joule's Law
Joule's law: H = I²Rt; heat produced ∝ I², R, and t
Applications: electric heater, electric iron, fuse wire, incandescent bulb
Fuse: melts when current exceeds safe limit; protects circuit
Thermoelectric Effects
Seebeck effect: EMF produced at junction of two dissimilar metals due to temperature difference; basis of thermocouple
Peltier effect: heat absorbed or liberated at junction when current flows; reverse of Seebeck
Thomson effect: heat absorbed or liberated in a single conductor with temperature gradient and current

chapters.title: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current

data.text: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current

kids.text: Introduction to Magnetism
Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel, unlike attract
Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist
Coulomb's law for magnets: F = µ₀/4π × (qm1 × qm2)/r²
Bar Magnet and Magnetic Dipole
Magnetic dipole moment: pm = qm × 2l; direction: S to N; unit: Am²
Axial field (end-on): B = µ₀/4π × 2pmr/(r²–l²)²
Equatorial field (broad-side): B = µ₀/4π × pm/(r²+l²)^(3/2); direction opposite to pm
Torque on dipole: τ = pmB sinθ
Potential energy: U = –pmB cosθ; minimum at θ = 0° (parallel)
Earth's Magnetism
Magnetic declination: angle between geographic and magnetic meridians
Magnetic dip (inclination): angle made by Earth's field with horizontal
Horizontal component: BH = B cosδ; Vertical component: BV = B sinδ
tan δ = BV/BH
Magnetic Properties of Materials
Magnetising field H: applied magnetic field; unit: Am⁻¹
Magnetic permeability µ: measure of ability to allow field lines; µᵣ = µ/µ₀
Magnetisation M: net magnetic moment per unit volume
Magnetic susceptibility χm = M/H; dimensionless
B = µ₀(H + M); total magnetic induction
Types of Magnetic Materials
Diamagnetic: χm small negative (e.g., copper, gold, bismuth); weakly repelled
Paramagnetic: χm small positive (e.g., aluminium, platinum); weakly attracted
Ferromagnetic: χm very large positive (e.g., iron, nickel, cobalt); strongly attracted
Hysteresis: lag of B behind H in ferromagnets; area of loop = energy loss per cycle
Retentivity: residual magnetism after removing H; Coercivity: H needed to demagnetize
Curie's law: χm ∝ 1/T for paramagnets; Curie-Weiss law for ferromagnets
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
Oersted's experiment: current-carrying wire deflects compass needle
Biot-Savart Law
dB = µ₀/4π × I dl sinθ/r²; magnetic field due to current element
For straight infinite wire: B = µ₀I/2πr
For circular loop at centre: B = µ₀I/2R
Ampère's Circuital Law
∮B·dl = µ₀I_enclosed; line integral of B around closed loop
Solenoid: B = µ₀nI (inside); n = N/L turns per unit length
Toroid: B = µ₀NI/2πr; zero outside
Force on a Moving Charge
Lorentz force: F = q(E + v × B)
Magnetic force: F = qvB sinθ; maximum when v ⊥ B
Circular motion in magnetic field: radius r = mv/qB; time period T = 2πm/qB
Velocity selector: qE = qvB ⟹ v = E/B
Cyclotron: particle accelerator using resonance condition; νc = qB/2πm
Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
F = BIl sinθ; Fleming's left hand rule gives direction
Force between parallel wires: F/l = µ₀I₁I₂/2πd; parallel currents attract
Definition of Ampere: force between two wires carrying equal currents
Torque on a Current Loop – Galvanometer
Torque: τ = NBIA sinθ; N turns, B field, I current, A area
Magnetic dipole moment of coil: m = NIA
Moving coil galvanometer: τ = kφ; deflection ∝ current
Ammeter: galvanometer + low shunt resistance in parallel
Voltmeter: galvanometer + high resistance in series
Magnetic Moment and Gyromagnetic Ratio
Orbital magnetic moment of electron: µL = –(e/2m)L
Gyromagnetic ratio: µL/L = e/2m
Bohr magneton: µB = eh/4πm = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ Am²; minimum unit of magnetic moment
Electromagnetic Induction
Faraday's experiment: changing magnetic flux induces EMF in a coil
Faraday's Laws
First law: EMF is induced whenever magnetic flux through a circuit changes
Second law: induced EMF ε = –dΦB/dt (magnitude ∝ rate of change of flux)
Magnetic flux: ΦB = B·A = BA cosθ; unit: Weber (Wb)
Lenz's Law
Induced current opposes the cause producing it
Consistent with conservation of energy; prevents perpetual motion
Fleming's right hand rule: gives direction of induced current in moving conductor
Motional EMF: ε = Blv (conductor moving in magnetic field)
Motional EMF from Lorentz force: free electrons experience force, accumulate, create potential
Eddy Currents
Currents induced in bulk conductors by changing magnetic flux
Applications: electromagnetic braking, induction furnace, speedometer
Minimised by laminating core with insulating sheets
Self-Induction
EMF induced in a coil due to change in its own current
Coefficient of self-induction: L = NΦB/I; ε = –L(dI/dt)
Self-inductance of solenoid: L = µ₀N²A/l
Energy stored in inductor: U = ½LI²
Mutual Induction
EMF induced in secondary due to change in primary current
Coefficient of mutual induction: M = NₛΦs/Ip; ε₂ = –M(dI₁/dt)
For coaxial solenoids: M = µ₀N₁N₂A/l
AC Generator (Alternator)
Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy using electromagnetic induction
ε = NBAω sinωt = ε₀ sinωt; where ε₀ = NBAω is peak EMF
Three-phase AC generator: three coils 120° apart; used for power transmission
Alternating Current
v = Vm sinωt; i = Im sinωt; alternates direction periodically
RMS values: Vrms = Vm/√2; Irms = Im/√2
Mean (average) value: Vav = 2Vm/π (over half cycle)
AC in Different Circuit Elements
Resistive circuit: V and I in phase; P = I²R
Inductive circuit: I lags V by π/2; XL = ωL; P = 0 (wattless current)
Capacitive circuit: I leads V by π/2; XC = 1/ωC; P = 0 (wattless current)
Series RLC Circuit
Impedance: Z = √(R² + (XL – XC)²)
Phase angle: tan φ = (XL – XC)/R
Resonance: XL = XC ⟹ ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Z = R (minimum), I = maximum
Q-factor (sharpness): Q = ω₀L/R = 1/ω₀CR
Power in AC: P = Vrms × Irms × cosφ; cosφ = power factor
Wattless current: I sinφ component; produces no power
Transformer
Works on mutual induction; transfers energy between two circuits
Transformation ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is
Step-up: Ns > Np (increases voltage, decreases current)
Step-down: Ns < Np (decreases voltage, increases current)
Efficiency: η = (output power/input power) × 100%; losses: copper loss, iron loss, flux leakage
Used in long-distance power transmission to reduce I²R losses
Displacement Current and Maxwell's Correction
Ampere's law inconsistency: B field between capacitor plates not explained by conduction current alone
Displacement current: id = ε₀ dΦE/dt; produced by changing electric field
Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(Ic + id) = µ₀Ic + µ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt
Symmetry: changing B produces E (Faraday); changing E produces B (Maxwell)
Maxwell's Equations (Integral Form)
1st equation (Gauss's law for E): ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; electric field lines start and end on charges
2nd equation (Gauss's law for B): ∮B·dA = 0; no magnetic monopoles; field lines closed loops
3rd equation (Faraday's law): ∮E·dl = –dΦB/dt; changing B induces E
4th equation (Ampere-Maxwell): ∮B·dl = µ₀(Ic + ε₀dΦE/dt); both currents produce B
Electromagnetic Waves
Produced by oscillating electric charges (accelerating charges)
Transverse waves: E and B perpendicular to each other and to direction of propagation
Speed in vacuum: c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) = 3 × 10⁸ ms⁻¹; E₀/B₀ = c
In medium: v = c/n = 1/√(µε); n = √(εᵣµᵣ)
Properties of EM Waves
Not deflected by electric or magnetic field
Carry energy, linear momentum and angular momentum
Exhibit interference, diffraction and polarization
Do not require medium (non-mechanical waves)
Electromagnetic Spectrum
Radio waves: Hz to 10⁹ Hz; communication (TV, radio, cellular)
Microwaves: 10⁹ to 10¹¹ Hz; radar, satellite communication, microwave oven
Infrared (IR): 10¹¹ to 4×10¹⁴ Hz; heat, night vision, TV remotes, greenhouse effect
Visible light: 4×10¹⁴ to 7×10¹⁴ Hz; wavelength 400–700 nm
Ultraviolet (UV): 7×10¹⁴ to 10¹⁷ Hz; sterilization, causes sunburn, vitamin D production
X-rays: 10¹⁷ to 10¹⁹ Hz; medical imaging, crystal structure analysis
Gamma rays: 10¹⁹ Hz+; radioactive decay, cancer treatment, highest energy
Fraunhofer lines: dark absorption lines in solar spectrum; identify elements in the Sun
Hertz's Experiment
First experimental demonstration of EM waves (1887)
LC oscillator circuit produces EM waves; detected by ring detector
Confirmed Maxwell's predictions about EM waves
Nature of Light and Reflection
Ray optics: light represented as rays travelling in straight lines
Laws of reflection: i = r; incident ray, reflected ray and normal are coplanar
Angle of deviation in reflection: d = 180° – 2i (or d = 2α, where α is glancing angle)
Plane Mirror
Image is virtual, erect, same size as object, laterally inverted
Image distance = Object distance (behind mirror)
When mirror tilted by θ, reflected ray rotates by 2θ
Spherical Mirrors
Concave (converging) and convex (diverging) mirrors
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R (sign convention: distances measured from pole)
Magnification: m = –v/u; negative for real inverted image
Image formation by concave mirror
Object at infinity → real image at F (focal point)
Object between F and C → real, inverted, magnified image beyond C
Object at C → real, inverted, same size image at C
Object between P and F → virtual, erect, magnified image behind mirror
Refraction of Light
Bending of light at boundary of two media due to change in speed
Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂; refractive index n = c/v
Total internal reflection: when angle of incidence > critical angle (ic); n₂ sinic = n₁
Applications of TIR: optical fibre, diamond brilliance, mirage, looming
Optical fibres: light confined by TIR; used in endoscopy and communication
Refraction at Spherical Surfaces
n₂/v – n₁/u = (n₂–n₁)/R; refraction formula for spherical surface
Lensmaker's equation: 1/f = (n–1)[1/R₁ – 1/R₂]
Thin Lenses
Convex (converging) and concave (diverging) lenses
Lens formula: 1/v – 1/u = 1/f
Magnification: m = v/u = hi/ho
Power of lens: P = 1/f (in metres); unit: Dioptre (D)
Combination of lenses in contact: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂; P = P₁ + P₂
Prism and Dispersion
Deviation by prism: d = (i₁ + i₂) – A; A is prism angle
At minimum deviation: i₁ = i₂; n = sin[(A+D)/2] / sin(A/2)
Dispersion: splitting of white light into spectrum (VIBGYOR); violet deviates most
Angular dispersion: δv – δr; dispersive power: ω = (δv – δr)/δy
Scattering of light: Rayleigh scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴; blue sky, red sunrise/sunset
Optical Instruments
Simple microscope: convex lens; m = 1 + D/f (near point); m = D/f (normal focusing)
Compound microscope: objective (short focal length) + eyepiece; m = (L/fo)(D/fe)
Astronomical telescope: objective (long fo) + eyepiece (short fe); m = fo/fe
Terrestrial telescope: additional erecting lens for upright image
Reflecting telescope (Cassegrain): uses concave mirror objective; free from chromatic aberration
Defects of Vision
Myopia (nearsightedness): image in front of retina; corrected by concave lens (f = –x)
Hypermetropia (farsightedness): image behind retina; corrected by convex lens
Presbyopia: aging-related farsightedness; ciliary muscles weaken
Astigmatism: different curvatures in different planes of eye lens; corrected by cylindrical lens
Wave Nature of Light
Corpuscular theory (Newton): light as particles; fails to explain interference
Wave theory (Huygens): light as waves; explains interference and diffraction
Electromagnetic theory (Maxwell): light is EM wave; c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀)
Quantum theory (Planck, Einstein): light as photons; explains photoelectric effect
Huygens' Principle
Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets
New wavefront = common tangent to all secondary wavelets
Point source → spherical wavefront; source at infinity → plane wavefront
Explains reflection and refraction using wavefront concept
Interference of Light
Superposition of two coherent waves; constructive (bright) or destructive (dark) interference
Coherent sources: same frequency, same phase or constant phase difference, same waveform
Methods: wavefront division, intensity division, source and images
Young's Double Slit Experiment
Bright fringe position: yn = nλD/d
Dark fringe position: yn = (2n–1)λD/2d
Fringe width: β = λD/d (uniform spacing)
With white light: central fringe white; coloured fringes on sides
Interference in thin films: colours due to path difference 2µd; reflected: 2µd = (2n–1)λ/2
Imax = (√I₁ + √I₂)²; Imin = (√I₁ – √I₂)²
Diffraction
Bending of waves around sharp edges into geometrically shadowed region
Prominent when obstacle size ≈ wavelength of light
Types of Diffraction
Fresnel diffraction: spherical/cylindrical wavefront; source at finite distance
Fraunhofer diffraction: plane wavefront; source at infinity (or with lens)
Single slit diffraction: minima at a sinθ = nλ; central maximum widest and brightest
Fresnel's distance: zF = a²/λ; beyond this wave optics becomes important
Diffraction grating: (a+b) sinθ = mλ; used to determine wavelength with spectrometer
Resolution
Rayleigh's criterion: two objects just resolved when central max of one coincides with 1st min of other
Angular resolution of telescope: θ = 1.22λ/a; a = aperture diameter
Resolving power of microscope: RP = 2NA/1.22λ; NA = n sinθ (numerical aperture)
Polarisation
Restriction of vibrations of light to one direction; transverse nature of light
Plane polarised, partially polarised, unpolarised light
Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ; intensity after analyser
Brewster's law: tan iB = n; at Brewster angle, reflected light is fully polarised
Double refraction: birefringent crystals split light into ordinary and extraordinary rays
Nicol prism: uses calcite crystal to produce plane polarised light (extraordinary ray)
Scattering: scattered light perpendicular to incident is plane polarised (e.g., Raman scattering)

chapters.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

data.text: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

kids.text: Electron Emission
Free electrons in metal cannot escape due to surface barrier (potential barrier)
Work function (φ₀): minimum energy to liberate an electron; unit: eV
Types of Electron Emission
Thermionic emission: by heating (e.g., vacuum tubes, CRT)
Field emission: by strong electric field
Photo electric emission: by electromagnetic radiation of suitable frequency
Secondary emission: by bombarding fast electrons
Photoelectric Effect
Hertz (1887): UV light makes spark more vigorous; first observation
Hallwachs: zinc plate loses charge on UV irradiation
Lenard: measured charge and velocity of photoelectrons
Laws of Photoelectric Effect
Emission only when ν ≥ ν₀ (threshold frequency); depends on material
Number of photoelectrons ∝ intensity of light
Maximum KE independent of intensity; depends on frequency
No time lag between incidence and emission (< 10⁻⁹ s)
Stopping potential V₀: eV₀ = ½mv²max; independent of intensity
Failure of classical wave theory to explain photoelectric effect
Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
Light consists of photons; each photon has energy E = hν
Einstein's equation: ½mv²max = hν – φ₀ = h(ν – ν₀)
Threshold frequency: ν₀ = φ₀/h; threshold wavelength: λ₀ = hc/φ₀
Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js; determined from slope of V₀ vs ν graph
Particle Nature of Light – Photon
Photon: quantum of electromagnetic radiation; travels at speed c
Energy: E = hν = hc/λ; momentum: p = h/λ = E/c
Rest mass = 0; no charge
Compton effect: photon scattering proves particle nature; Δλ = (h/mec)(1–cosφ)
Wave Nature of Matter – de Broglie Hypothesis
de Broglie: matter has wave properties; λ = h/p = h/mv
de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/√(2mK); K is kinetic energy
For accelerated particle: λ = h/√(2meV)
Davisson-Germer experiment: electron diffraction by nickel crystal; confirmed wave nature
Wave-Particle Duality
Both radiation and matter exhibit dual nature depending on the experiment
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π; cannot simultaneously know both exactly
Electron microscope: uses de Broglie wavelength of electrons (much smaller than visible light) for higher resolution
Atomic Models
J.J. Thomson model (plum pudding/watermelon): uniform positive sphere with embedded electrons; failed to explain line spectra
Rutherford Model (1911)
Alpha particle scattering by gold foil (Geiger-Marsden experiment)
Atom mostly empty space; nucleus is small, dense, positively charged
Electrons revolve around nucleus
Distance of closest approach: r₀ = Ze²/4πε₀Ek
Impact parameter: related to scattering angle; larger b → smaller deflection
Limitations: cannot explain stability (spiral in) or discrete line spectrum
Bohr Model of Hydrogen Atom
Postulate 1: electrons revolve in stable circular orbits (stationary orbits) without radiating
Postulate 2: angular momentum quantized: mvr = nh/2π
Postulate 3: energy emitted/absorbed = hν = E₂ – E₁ when electron jumps orbit
Radius of nth orbit: rn = n²a₀/Z; a₀ = 0.529 Å (Bohr radius)
Energy of nth orbit: En = –13.6Z²/n² eV; ground state n=1, E₁ = –13.6 eV for H
Velocity in nth orbit: vn = (Z/n) × 2.19 × 10⁶ ms⁻¹
Limitations: cannot explain multi-electron atoms, fine structure, Zeeman effect
Hydrogen Spectrum
Line emission spectrum: discrete wavelengths emitted when electrons transition between orbits
Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R[1/n₁² – 1/n₂²]; R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
Spectral Series
Lyman series: n₁=1; UV region
Balmer series: n₁=2; visible region (Hα, Hβ, Hγ, Hδ)
Paschen series: n₁=3; near IR region
Brackett series: n₁=4; IR region
Pfund series: n₁=5; far IR region
Ionisation energy of hydrogen: 13.6 eV; ionisation potential: 13.6 V
Excitation energy: energy needed to move electron from ground state to excited state
Nucleus
Nucleus contains protons (Z) and neutrons (N); A = Z + N (mass number)
Nuclear size: R = R₀A^(1/3); R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m; nuclear density ≈ constant for all nuclei
Isotopes: same Z, different A; Isobars: same A, different Z; Isotones: same N
Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c²
Mass defect: Δm = Zmp + Nmn – M (actual mass always less than sum of parts)
Binding energy: BE = Δm × c²; energy needed to completely separate nucleons
Binding energy per nucleon: BE/A; peaks near Fe-56; basis for fusion and fission
Radioactivity
Spontaneous disintegration of unstable nuclei; discovered by Becquerel (1896)
Types of Radioactive Decay
Alpha decay: emits ⁴₂He nucleus; Z decreases by 2, A by 4
Beta decay (β⁻): emits electron + antineutrino; neutron → proton; Z increases by 1
Beta+ decay: emits positron + neutrino; proton → neutron; Z decreases by 1
Gamma decay: emits high energy photon; no change in Z or A; nucleus de-excites
Radioactive decay law: N = N₀e^(–λt); λ is decay constant
Half-life: T½ = 0.693/λ; time for half the atoms to decay
Mean life: τ = 1/λ = T½/0.693
Activity: A = λN = A₀e^(–λt); unit: Becquerel (Bq) = 1 decay/s; also Curie (Ci)
Nuclear Reactions
Nuclear Fission
Heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei; releases huge energy (200 MeV per fission)
Example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + energy
Chain reaction: neutrons from fission trigger further fissions; controlled in reactor, uncontrolled in bomb
Critical mass: minimum mass needed for sustained chain reaction
Nuclear Fusion
Light nuclei fuse to form heavier nucleus; releases more energy per unit mass than fission
Example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV
Requires extremely high temperature (10⁷ K); thermonuclear reaction; source of stellar energy
Nuclear reactor: moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons; coolant removes heat
Elementary Particles
Quarks: fundamental building blocks of hadrons; proton = uud, neutron = udd
Leptons: electrons, neutrinos, muons; not affected by strong force
Four fundamental forces: gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear, weak nuclear
Energy Band Theory
Valence band: highest filled energy band at 0 K
Conduction band: partially filled or empty; electrons here contribute to conductivity
Band gap (Eg): energy gap between valence and conduction bands
Classification of Solids by Band Gap
Conductors: overlapping bands or half-filled conduction band; Eg ≈ 0
Semiconductors: small Eg (≈ 1 eV); Si (1.1 eV), Ge (0.7 eV)
Insulators: large Eg (> 3 eV); electrons cannot cross to conduction band
Semiconductors
Intrinsic semiconductor: pure Si or Ge; ni = pi; conductivity increases with temperature
Extrinsic Semiconductors (Doping)
n-type: doped with pentavalent (donor) impurity (e.g., As, P); electrons are majority carriers
p-type: doped with trivalent (acceptor) impurity (e.g., B, Al); holes are majority carriers
Conductivity: σ = e(neµe + nhµh); µ = mobility
p-n Junction Diode
Depletion region: region near junction depleted of mobile charges; creates built-in potential
Forward bias: p connected to +ve, n to –ve; depletion layer narrows; current flows
Reverse bias: p connected to –ve, n to +ve; depletion layer widens; only small leakage current
V-I characteristics: exponential in forward bias; nearly zero in reverse bias until breakdown
Rectifier: converts AC to DC; half-wave or full-wave (bridge); filter smooths output
Special Diodes
Zener diode: operates in reverse breakdown; used as voltage regulator
LED (Light Emitting Diode): forward biased; emits photons when electrons recombine with holes; E = hν
Photodiode: reverse biased; generates current proportional to incident light intensity
Solar cell: unbiased p-n junction; converts solar energy to electrical energy
Transistor
Three-layer (p-n-p or n-p-n) semiconductor device; emitter, base, collector
Emitter-base: forward biased; collector-base: reverse biased
Current relations: IE = IB + IC; α = IC/IE; β = IC/IB; β = α/(1–α)
Common emitter configuration: voltage gain = β × Rc/Ri; input and output 180° out of phase
Transistor as switch: saturation (ON) and cut-off (OFF) regions
Transistor as oscillator: uses positive feedback; sustains oscillations
Digital Electronics
Binary system: two states 0 and 1 (LOW and HIGH voltage)
Boolean algebra: AND (·), OR (+), NOT (̄); De Morgan's theorems
Logic Gates
AND gate: output 1 only when all inputs are 1; Y = A·B
OR gate: output 1 when any input is 1; Y = A+B
NOT gate: output is complement of input; Y = Ā
NAND gate: NOT AND; universal gate; Y = ̄(A·B)
NOR gate: NOT OR; universal gate; Y = ̄(A+B)
XOR gate: output 1 when inputs differ; Y = A⊕B
Communication Systems
Basic elements: transmitter, channel (medium), receiver
Signal, noise, bandwidth, range: key parameters
Modulation
AM (Amplitude Modulation): amplitude of carrier varies with signal; µ = Am/Ac; bandwidth = 2fm
FM (Frequency Modulation): frequency of carrier varies; less noise; used in FM radio
PM (Phase Modulation): phase of carrier varies with signal
Demodulation: recovery of original signal from modulated carrier
Ground wave propagation: follows Earth's surface; up to 2 MHz
Sky wave (ionospheric) propagation: reflected by ionosphere; for HF (3–30 MHz)
Space wave propagation: line of sight; for VHF and above; TV, satellite
Satellite communication: uses geostationary satellites at 36,000 km altitude
Mobile telephony: cellular network, multiple access, SIM cards
Internet and broadband: optical fibre, WiFi, 4G/5G
Nanotechnology
Science and technology of materials at nanoscale (1–100 nm)
Feynman's vision (1959): 'There's plenty of room at the bottom'
Properties change drastically at nanoscale (surface area : volume ratio increases)
Nanoparticles: gold nanoparticles appear red/purple (not gold) due to quantum effects
Carbon Nanostructures
Carbon nanotubes (CNT): cylindrical rolled graphene; remarkable electrical and mechanical properties
Fullerenes (C60): spherical cage molecule (Buckminsterfullerene); like a soccer ball
Graphene: single layer of graphite; strongest material; excellent conductor; 2D material
Tools: STM (Scanning Tunnelling Microscope) – images individual atoms
Applications of Nanotechnology
Medicine: targeted drug delivery, cancer treatment, nano-robots
Electronics: transistors at nano level; denser integrated circuits
Energy: solar cells, fuel cells, hydrogen storage
Materials: nanocomposites, scratch-resistant coatings, nano-filters
Robotics
Study and application of robots; interdisciplinary: electronics, mechanics, computing
Components: sensors, actuators, controller, power supply, end-effector
Types: industrial, medical (surgical robots), space (rovers), domestic
Degrees of freedom (DOF): number of independent movements possible
AI and machine learning enable autonomous robots
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Simulation of human intelligence processes by machines
Machine Learning: computers learn from data without explicit programming
Deep Learning: multi-layer neural networks; image recognition, NLP
Applications: medical diagnosis, weather prediction, autonomous vehicles, language translation
Gravitational Waves
Ripples in space-time caused by accelerating massive objects; predicted by Einstein (1916)
First detected by LIGO (2015) from merger of two black holes; Nobel Prize 2017
Travel at speed of light; extremely weak (stretch/compress space by 10⁻²¹ m)
Sources: merging neutron stars, black holes, supernovae
Superconductivity
Zero electrical resistance below critical temperature (Tc)
Discovered by Kamerlingh Onnes (1911) in mercury at 4.2 K
Meissner effect: perfect diamagnetism; expels magnetic field (B = 0 inside)
BCS theory: Cooper pairs of electrons; phonon-mediated interaction
High-temperature superconductors: ceramic compounds with Tc above 77 K (liquid nitrogen)
Applications: MRI machines, maglev trains, SQUID, particle accelerators (LHC)
Big Bang and Cosmology
Big Bang theory: universe originated ~13.8 billion years ago from extremely hot, dense singularity
Hubble's law: v = Hd; galaxies recede with velocity ∝ distance; H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc
CMB (Cosmic Microwave Background): relic radiation at 2.7 K; evidence for Big Bang
Dark matter: 27% of universe; doesn't interact with light; detected via gravitational effects
Dark energy: 68% of universe; causes accelerated expansion
Black holes: extremely dense objects; escape velocity exceeds c; event horizon
